prompt: Which statement best describes an Availability Zone?

options.text: One or more discrete data centers with redundant power, networking, and connectivity in a Region
options.explanation: Correct. This is how AWS defines an Availability Zone.

options.text: A geographic grouping of several Regions
options.explanation: The relationship is the other way round: a Region contains Availability Zones.

options.text: A site that caches content close to users
options.explanation: That describes an edge location, which Amazon CloudFront uses to deliver content.

options.text: A single server that AWS assigns to one customer
options.explanation: An Availability Zone is data center infrastructure shared by many customers, not one server.

explanation: A Region is a physical location where AWS clusters data centers. Each Availability Zone within it is one or more discrete data centers with redundant power, networking, and connectivity.

prompt: An online retailer runs its website on servers in one Availability Zone. A power failure in that Availability Zone takes the website offline. What is the most direct way to reduce the impact of a similar failure?

options.text: Run the website across multiple Availability Zones in the Region
options.explanation: Correct. Availability Zones do not share single points of failure such as generators and cooling equipment, so the website can keep running in another zone.

options.text: Move the website to a larger server in the same Availability Zone
options.explanation: A larger server adds capacity, but it still depends on the same Availability Zone.

options.text: Add more edge locations to the Availability Zone
options.explanation: Edge locations are not part of an Availability Zone, and customers do not add them.

options.text: Upgrade the AWS Support plan
options.explanation: A support plan gives access to help. It does not change how the website is deployed.

explanation: High availability comes from removing single points of failure. Running across multiple Availability Zones means a failure in one zone does not have to stop the application.

references.title: AWS Fault Isolation Boundaries: Availability Zones

prompt: Which TWO are valid reasons for a company to use more than one AWS Region?

options.text: Disaster recovery and business continuity
options.explanation: Correct. A second Region gives a company somewhere to recover if a whole Region is affected.

options.text: Lower latency for users in different parts of the world
options.explanation: Correct. Selecting a Region close to users lowers network latency.

options.text: Moving security responsibility for its data to AWS
options.explanation: Customers remain responsible for security in the cloud, whichever Regions they use.

options.text: Avoiding the need for Availability Zones
options.explanation: Every Region is made up of Availability Zones, so using more Regions does not remove them.

options.text: Using AWS services without charge
options.explanation: Using another Region does not make services free.

explanation: The exam guide lists disaster recovery, business continuity, low latency for end users, and data sovereignty as reasons to use multiple Regions.

prompt: A media company stores video thumbnails in one AWS Region. Viewers on other continents report that the images load slowly. Which AWS capability is designed to deliver this content with lower latency?

options.text: Amazon CloudFront edge locations
options.explanation: Correct. CloudFront routes each request to the edge location with the lowest latency and can serve cached copies of files from there.

options.text: Additional Availability Zones in the same Region
options.explanation: More Availability Zones improve availability. They do not move content closer to viewers on other continents.

options.text: A larger Amazon EC2 instance
options.explanation: A larger server does not shorten the distance between the content and distant viewers.

options.text: A higher AWS Support plan
options.explanation: Support plans provide access to help. They do not change how content is delivered.

explanation: Edge locations exist to deliver content close to users. Caching copies of files there reduces the delay for users who are far from the origin.

prompt: A company is choosing an AWS Region for a new application. Which TWO factors should influence the decision?

options.text: Whether the Region offers the AWS services and features the application needs
options.explanation: Correct. AWS advises selecting a Region that has the services and features you need.

options.text: How close the Region is to most of the application's users
options.explanation: Correct. A Region close to most users lowers network latency.

options.text: How long the company has held its AWS account
options.explanation: Account age is not a factor in choosing a Region.

options.text: Whether the Region makes Availability Zones free of charge
options.explanation: Availability Zones are part of every Region and are not a way to avoid charges.

options.text: Which Region stores the root user's password
options.explanation: This is not a factor in choosing where to run an application.

explanation: Service availability and proximity to users both matter. Regulatory, compliance, and legal requirements can also determine the choice.

prompt: Why can an application that runs in two Availability Zones keep working when one of them has a power failure?

options.text: Availability Zones do not share common points of failure such as generators and cooling equipment
options.explanation: Correct. This independence means a failure in one Availability Zone should not take down another.

options.text: Both Availability Zones are in the same building, so power can be switched between them
options.explanation: Availability Zones are physically separated by a meaningful distance.

options.text: Each Availability Zone is in a different Region
options.explanation: Availability Zones are inside a Region. A Region contains several of them.

options.text: Edge locations automatically run the application during a failure
options.explanation: Edge locations deliver content close to users. They do not take over running the application in this way.

explanation: AWS designs Availability Zones so that common points of failure are not shared, and they are physically separated while linked by low-latency networking.
